# Why Communication Is KT {.unnumbered}

## Where This Fits

You already have descriptive evidence. A plot, a Table 1, and a dashboard prototype can all be technically correct and still fail if the intended audience cannot tell what matters.

<!-- AI-EDIT(2026-06-11): TF-025, MIT-089, WI-047 — needs review -->
Science communication means explaining scientific evidence clearly and responsibly for a specific audience. In this course, that means turning one audited health data finding into a short, plain-language message that includes evidence, limitations, and appropriate caution.

Communication is part of knowledge translation. It turns evidence into a form that helps a person make sense of a question, ask a better follow-up, or avoid a bad interpretation.

## The Week 9 Task

This week asks for one small communication product:

- one audience;
- one question;
- one figure, table, or dashboard output;
- one plain-language takeaway;
- one limitation;
- one source note.

That is enough. More slides are not automatically better.

<!-- AI-EDIT(2026-06-11): TF-026, MIT-090, WI-048 — needs review -->
## Match the Message to the Audience

Before writing, identify your audience: experts may need methods, policymakers may need decision relevance, patients may need clear practical meaning, and the public may need plain language and careful context.

| Audience | What they usually need | What that means for your message |
|---|---|---|
| Experts (analysts, researchers) | Methods and definitions | Name the data source, the variables, and how groups were formed |
| Policymakers | Decision relevance | Lead with the takeaway and say what decision or discussion it informs |
| Patients | Clear practical meaning | Explain what the finding means in everyday terms, without causing alarm |
| General public | Plain language and careful context | Avoid jargon and keep the limitation right next to the claim |

The finding and the evidence stay the same. What changes is the emphasis, the wording, and how much technical detail you show.

## What Counts as Evidence

Use work from earlier weeks:

| Earlier artifact | How it can support Week 9 |
|---|---|
| A5 corrected plot | Evidence slide or visual example |
| A5 caption | Source, statistic, exclusion, and limitation wording |
| A6 Table 1 | Descriptive context or supporting table |
| A6 methods note | Data and cohort explanation |
| A6 provenance note | Source and stewardship note |
| A7 dashboard adaptation | Audience and KT purpose |
| A7 limitation/privacy check | Caution slide or speaker note |

## Keep the Claim Small

Good Week 9 claims sound like this:

> In this prepared classroom dataset, mean BMI differs across income groups, but the comparison is descriptive and unweighted.

Weak Week 9 claims sound like this:

> Income causes BMI differences.

The second claim is not supported by the course workflow. The first claim is cautious, understandable, and grounded in the evidence students have actually produced.

## AI Use

AI may help simplify wording, draft speaker notes, or suggest slide order. It must not invent sources, make results stronger than the code supports, or remove limitations to make a message sound cleaner.

## Check Yourself

Before moving on, answer:

- Who is the audience?
- What decision, conversation, or question does the communication support?
- Which prior artifact is the evidence?
- What limitation must remain visible?
